## Background

There was well-documented racial disparity in postoperative complications in hysterectomy patients. We were interested in intraoperative factors and surgical factors that may contribute to the racial disparity. The knowledge may help develop programs addressing racial disparity.

## Study population

MSQC hysterectomy patients 2015-2018 (N=27,369).

Exclusion criteria:

-cancer patients

-race group \<=1%

-missing values

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(DiagrammeR)
grViz("digraph flowchart {
      # node definitions with substituted label text
      node [fontname = Helvetica, shape = rectangle]        
      tab1 [label = '@@1']
      tab2 [label = '@@2']
      tab3 [label = '@@3']
      tab4 [label = '@@4']

      # edge definitions with the node IDs
      tab1 -> tab2 -> tab3 -> tab4 -> tab5;
      }

      [1]: 'MSQC hysterectomy patients 2015-2018 (N=27,369)'
      [2]: 'Benign N=21,214'

      [4]: 'Participants had complete data  N=18,395'
      [5]: 'Study population N=18,395'
      ")
```

## Objective

To evaluate clinical factors that are associated with racial disparities in major postoperative complications.

## Primary outcome

Major postoperative complications including deep incision/organ ssi, sepsis, septic shock, major cardiovascular complications, pneumonia, and venous thromboembolism.

## Variables of interest

-Demographic and clinical characteristics:  age, race, BMI, insurance, hospital teaching status, hospital size, ASA class, comorbidities, hematocrit, uterine weight.  

-Intraoperative characteristics: appropriate documentation, preferred antibiotics, abdominal preparation, intraoperative warming, bleeding barrier, perioperative mechanical DVT prophylaxis, Perioperative pharmacological DVT prophylaxis, multimodal pain management.

-Surgical characteristics: surgeon volume, surgery time, surgical approach, same day discharge.

## Methods

Continuous variables were presented in median(IQR) and categorical variables were presented in numbers and percentages. Pearson's Chi-squared test, Fisher's exact, and Wilcoxon rank sum tests were performed. Two-sided p\<0.05 was defined as significant. All data management and analyses were performed using R (version 4.3.0).

## 

Risk factors for major postoperative complications

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(gtsummary)
library(forcats)
library(rio)
require(lme4)
require(broom.mixed)
# read rds
data2 <- readRDS("data2.rds")
# descriptive summary
data2 |>  
  select(calculated_age, bmi, bmigroup1, race1, e_teaching, e_beds, insurance,
         flg_cmb_sleep_apnea, flg_cmb_diabetes,	flg_cmb_hypertension,	flg_cmb_smoker,	flg_cmb_dvt, functional,	flg_cmb_coronary_artery, asaclass, hct_no, ebl,hct, specmn_weight_grams,  uterine, flg_w_h_cmplt_pap, flg_w_h_cmplt_biopsy, 
cmplt_image, skin, mech_periop_vte_prophylaxis, pharm_periop_vte_prophylaxis,	
bleeding_barrier,	prefer, intraop_warming,	flg_intraop_multimodal_pain_med, volume, hb_mis, mis_open, mis_uterine, open_uterine, bleeding_barrier, surgery_time, sameday, cmp_anymajor1) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by=cmp_anymajor1) |>
  add_p() |>
  modify_header(
    stat_1 ~ "**No**",
    stat_2 ~ "**Yes**"
  ) |> 
  modify_spanning_header(all_stat_cols() ~ "**Major postoperative complications**")
```

Significant risk factors identified (p\<.01): BMI, race, insurance, comorbidities (diabetes, DVT), ASA class, anemia, uterine weight, imaging documentation, bleeding barrier, preferred antibiotics, surgeon volume, surgery time, surgical approach, same day discharge (risk factor or outcome?). Among these risk factors, we were particularly interested in race, if there was racial disparity in secondary outcomes (readmission, transfusion, same day discharge, ED visits), and what covariates contributed to the racial disparity in major postoperative complication rates.

## Secondary outcomes in White and Black patients

```{r}
#| echo: false
data2 |>
  select(race1, cmp_anymajor1, cmp_ssi, cmp_sep, cmp_ssep, cmp_pn, cmp_cardivas, cmp_vte, event_edorur, event_return, sameday, cmp_trans,event_readmit)|>
   tbl_summary(
    by=race1,
    missing = "no",
    label=sameday ~ "Same day discharge",
    digits = list(all_categorical() ~ c(0, 1)))|>
  add_p() |>
  add_ci() |>
  modify_spanning_header(
    all_stat_cols() ~ "**Hysterectomy Patients**") |>
  modify_caption("**Postop Characteristics**")
```

## Unmodifiable and modifiable factors

We then categorized significant risk factors into unmodifiable and modifiable factors (surgeons' decision-making). Unmodifiable factors included BMI, ASA class, anemia, uterine weight, comorbidities (diabetes, DVT) and insurance.

Modifiable factors included intraoperative events such as appropriate imaging documentation, preferred antibiotics, bleeding barrier, and surgical events such as surgeon volume, surgery time, and surgical approach. This knowledge could have implications to develop programs addressing disparities.

## Bivariate analysis: unmodifiable events

```{r}
#| echo: false
data2 |>
  select(race1, bmi, bmigroup1, insurance, flg_cmb_diabetes,	flg_cmb_dvt,
        asaclass, ebl,  hct, specmn_weight_grams,  uterine) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by=race1,
    # missing = "no",
    digits = list(all_categorical() ~ c(0, 1)))|>
  add_p()
```

## Bivariate analysis: modifiable events

```{r}
#| echo: false
data2 |>
  select(race1, bmi, bmigroup1, insurance, flg_cmb_diabetes,	flg_cmb_dvt,
        asaclass, ebl,  hct, specmn_weight_grams,  uterine) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by=race1,
    # missing = "no",
    digits = list(all_categorical() ~ c(0, 1)))|>
    add_p() 
```

Black patients had higher rates of appropriate imaging documentation and preferred antibiotics compared to White patients.

These modifiable factors may contribute to the racial disparity: bleeding barrier, surgical approach, operative time, and surgeon volume.

## Univariate logistic regression

A univariate logistic regression was used to investigate the association of variables including both unmodifiable and modifiable, and major postoperative complications. Considering ebl and anemia are highly correlated, only anemia was included. History of DVT was excluded due to the high rate of missing values. Categorical BMI and uterine weight were included.

```{r}
#| echo: false
data2 |>
  select(race1, bmigroup1, insurance, asaclass, flg_cmb_diabetes,  hct, uterine, 
         bleeding_barrier, volume, hb_mis, surgery_time, cmp_anymajor1) |>
  tbl_uvregression(method = glm, 
                   y= cmp_anymajor1,
                   method.args = list(family = binomial),
                   exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  #  add_global_p()|>
  modify_caption("**Univariate logistic regression**")
```

## Mixed effects logistic regression

Significant risk factors (p \<.01) were included in multiple logistic regression. Considering the random effect of the surgeon, a generalized linear model was used.  The random factor was the surgeon, other risk factors were fixed. The finalized model was mixed effects logistic regression.

Results: Black patients had increased odds of major postoperative complications compared to White patients after adjusting for BMI, ASA class, insurance, uterine weight, anemia, diabetes, bleeding barrier, surgical approach, surgery time, and random effect of surgeon (aOR 1.40, 95%CI 1.05-1.89, P=.024).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#full model
glmer(cmp_anymajor1 ~ race1 + bmigroup1 +  insurance + asaclass  + flg_cmb_diabetes
       + hct + uterine +  bleeding_barrier + hb_mis + surgery_time + 
        (1 | physician_cid), data=data2, family=binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"),
      nAGQ = 10)|>
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE)|>
  modify_caption("**Mixed effects logistic regression**") 

```

## Modifiable factors

To further understand how modifiable factors contributed to racial disparity in major postoperative complications, we first generated a baseline model that included unmodifiable factors only.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# base model
glm(cmp_anymajor1 ~ race1 + bmigroup1 +  insurance + asaclass  + flg_cmb_diabetes
      + hct + uterine, data=data2, family=binomial)|>
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE)
```

We then added individual modifiable factors and combinations to the baseline model. The adjusted odds ratios for race are listed in this table:![](images/Picture1.png)

## Conclusion

Our data suggested that combining minimal use of bleeding barrier, shortened operative time, and minimally invasive surgical approach may help address racial disparity in major postoperative complication rates.

response:

In terms of selecting variables:

-unfortunately, there is no definite answer to this question, it's a combination of clinical knowledge, public health science, statistics and common sense. This is hard......

-include statistically significant variables, but be careful for those too similar, or too closely related to each other. For example, surgical approach and ebl. I agree with Dr.Till's comments on these two variables, let's remove ebl;

-include clinically significant variables;

-have a theory for each variable included/excluded in the model. I like Dr. Till's comments on "insurance".

In terms of model performance:

-R2 is most commonly used as a measure of goodness of fit in linear regression;

For logistic regression model:

-Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit test could be used to evaluate individual models. A good fit (p\>=0.05) indicates that the estimated probabilities are in agreement with observed probabilities;

-Likelihood ratio test could be used to compare the goodness of fit of two models (full vs nested).

What I have done:

Model#1 (full): race, BMI, insurance, ASA, anemia, diabetes, uterine weight, op time, MIS approach, bleeding barrier, abx, surgeon volume

Model#2 (nested): race, BMI, ASA, anemia, diabetes, uterine weight, op time, MIS approach, bleeding barrier, abx, surgeon volume

1.  Hosmer-Lemeshow test on models:

    Model#1 p=0.27

Model#2 p=0.56

Interpretation: both models fit

2.  Likelihood ratio test:

    P=0.006

Interpretation: removing "insurance" significantly changes model fit, "insurance" should be added back. However, scientific context is more critical than measures.

Here is our final model:

race, BMI, ASA, anemia, diabetes, uterine weight, op time, MIS approach, bleeding barrier, abx, surgeon volume

### 05/09/2024 final thoughts

**theory of removing "insurance"**

Dr. Till "On a similar note, I'm wondering whether we should remove insurance type from the model? I know that there is data suggesting that insurance and complications are strongly associated, however it is not actually the insurance type that carries risk for complications. Rather, patients who are on public insurance have higher rates of medical comorbidities or social stressors that likely contribute to complication rates. Similarly, I suspect that patients with public insurance may have less access to high volume surgeons or MIS surgical approach than patients who are on commercial insurance."

**theory of removing "ebl"**

Dr. Till: "correlated with uterine size";

"MIS approach is a) more impactful on complication rate than EBL based on existing literature and b) more potentially modifiable than EBL."

correlated with anemia or surgical approach?

**Anemia: modifiable or non-modifiable?**

**theory of removing "tobacco"**

not statistically significant in bivariate analysis (White vs Black), but significant in bivariate analysis (major complication Yes or No)

clinically significant

statistically significant in univariate logistic regression, not significant in multivariable logistic regression (after adjusting for other risk factors)

**why removed:** have a weak association with the outcome (major complication), p=0.032; risk factors p \< 0.01 were included in multivariable logistic regression.

### 05/29/2025 resubmission

create tertiles for surgeon annual case volume:

low volume (1-33^th^ percentile), medium volume (34-66^th^ percentile), high volume (67^th^ percentile and above)

For example, in 2016, total 5,545 surgeries, 712 unique surgeons, tertile surgeries T1=3, T2=7, max=104. #surgeries \<=3-low, \>3 and \<=7 medium, \>7-high. among those, 242 (34%) are high volume surgeon, 170 (24%) are medium, 300 (42%) are low volume. Median number of surgeries by high, medium, low volume surgeons are 13, 5, 2. Total number of surgeries by high, medium, low volume surgeons are 4102, 896, 547.

```{r}
###calculate annual surgeon volume: tertile###
volume <-
  data2|>
  filter(surgery_year==2016)|> # do the same thing for 2016-2018
  select(physician_cid)|>
  group_by(physician_cid) |>
  summarise(
    frequency = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() 

volume <-
  volume|>
  summarise(
    q1 = quantile(frequency, 0.33),
    q2 = quantile(frequency, 0.66),
    q3 = max(frequency))
volume
#2015, 1, 3, 24
#2016, 3, 7, 104
#2017, 3, 9, 94
#2018, 4, 10, 90

s_all <-
  data2|>
  select(physician_cid)|>
  group_by(physician_cid) |>
  summarise(
    frequency = n()
  )  # total 898 surgeons
s2015 <-
  data2|>
  filter(surgery_year==2015)|>
  select(physician_cid)|>
  group_by(physician_cid) |>
  summarise(
    frequency = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(volume2015=case_when(frequency<=1 ~"low",
                              frequency<=3 ~"medium",
                               frequency>3 ~"high"))  

s2016 <-
  data2|>
  filter(surgery_year==2016)|>
  select(physician_cid)|>
  group_by(physician_cid) |>
  summarise(
    frequency = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(volume2016=case_when(frequency<=3 ~"low",
                              frequency<=7 ~"medium",
                           frequency>7 ~"high"))
#calculate #cases in each category
s2016 |>
  select(frequency,volume2016)|>
  tbl_summary(by=volume2016)
sum <- s2016 |> 
  select(frequency, volume2016) |> 
  group_by(volume2016) |> 
  summarise(
    total_frequency = sum(frequency) 
  ) |> 
  ungroup()
sum

s2017 <-
  data2|>
  filter(surgery_year==2017)|>
  select(physician_cid)|>
  group_by(physician_cid) |>
  summarise(
    frequency = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(volume2017=case_when(frequency<=3 ~"low",
                               frequency<=9 ~"medium",
                               frequency>9 ~"high"))

s2018 <-
  data2|>
  filter(surgery_year==2018)|>
  select(physician_cid)|>
  group_by(physician_cid) |>
  summarise(
    frequency = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(volume2018=case_when(frequency<=4 ~"low",
                               frequency<=10 ~"medium",
                               frequency>10 ~"high"))
test0 <-
  s2015 |>
  select(physician_cid, volume2015)|>
  full_join(s_all, s2015,by=join_by(physician_cid), relationship="many-to-many")

test <-
  s2016 |>
  select(physician_cid, volume2016)|>
  full_join(test0, s2016,by=join_by(physician_cid), relationship="many-to-many")

test1 <-
  s2017 |>
  select(physician_cid, volume2017)|>
  full_join(test, s2017,  by=join_by(physician_cid), relationship="many-to-many")

test2 <-
  s2018 |>
  select(physician_cid, volume2018)|>
  full_join(test1, s2018,  by=join_by(physician_cid), relationship="many-to-many")

data2 <-
  full_join(data2, test2,  by=join_by(physician_cid), relationship="many-to-many")

data2<-
  data2 |>
  mutate(volume_new=case_when(c(surgery_year==2015 & volume2015=="low")~"low",
                          c(surgery_year==2015 & volume2015=="medium")~"medium",                              c(surgery_year==2015 & volume2015=="high")~"high",
                          c(surgery_year==2016 & volume2016=="low")~"low",
                          c(surgery_year==2016 & volume2016=="medium")~"medium", 
                          c(surgery_year==2016 & volume2016=="high")~"high",
                          c(surgery_year==2017 & volume2017=="low")~"low",
                          c(surgery_year==2017 & volume2017=="medium")~"medium", 
                          c(surgery_year==2017 & volume2017=="high")~"high",
                          c(surgery_year==2018 & volume2018=="low")~"low",
                          c(surgery_year==2018 & volume2018=="medium")~"medium", 
                          c(surgery_year==2018 & volume2018=="high")~"high"))

library(Hmisc)
data2$volume_new <- forcats::fct_relevel(data2$volume_new, "high", "medium", "low")
label(data2$volume_new) <- "Surgeon volume"
#save dataset 
export(data2, "data2.rds")
```

Editor's questions:

2\) Please comment on the extent of missing data and how that was handled in the analysis.\
3) The methods section is well written, yet a few details are missing from the model building process. The final results are contingent on decisions made at each step, impacting interpretation of the findings and, potentially, reproducibility. Specifically:\
3a) Explain why not all factors associated with p\<0.05 in Table 1 are included in Table 3. If other criteria were applied, please describe in the methods (see lines 227-229).\
3b) Add the statistical criteria used in the backwards elimination process, e.g., p\<0.05, AIC, BIC, or something else.\
3c) If the focus was on identifying modifiable factors, did you consider forcing in important non-modifiable factors selected from the univariable models? For example, insurance seems to fall out but one could justify keeping it in the model anyway.

Responses:

2). Missing data:

We appreciate the editor’s question regarding missing data. To maintain the clarity and readability of our tables, we didn’t list the extent of missing data directly within them due to space constraints. We also didn’t perform imputation for missing data.

For reference, the following variables had complete data: age, BMI, race, teaching hospital, hospital size, insurance type, obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes, hypertension, tobacco use, coronary artery disease, ASA class, preop hematocrit value, anemia, uterine weight, bleeding barrier, preferred antibiotics administered, surgeon volume, surgical approach, MIS converted to open surgery, and operative times.

The estimated blood loss (EBL) variable had \<0.01% missing data.

History of DVT, appropriate abdominal prep, perioperative mechanical DVT prophylaxis, perioperative pharmacological DVT prophylaxis, and same day discharge all had 1-10% missing data.

Pap smear documented (17%), biopsy documented (17%), imaging documented (17%), prior pelvic surgery (37%), previous trials for symptom management (11%),  and intraop warming (31%) had \>10% missing data.

We will add appropriate notations in the relevant tables to indicate variables with \>10% missing data to further clarify this for readers.

3a).

Thank you for highlighting the need for clarification. We apologize for any confusion. All factors associated with p\<0.05 in Table 1 were included in Table 3. Table 1 is organized by demographic, clinical, perioperative clinical best practice, surgical, hospital and surgeon characteristics; Table 3 is structured to present results by nonmodifiable and modifiable factors, which may account for differences in presentation.

3b).

We utilized a backwards elimination process with a significance threshold of p\<0.05. We have added this detail to the Methods section for clarity.

3c).

We appreciate the reviewers and editor’s insightful comment about the inclusion of important nonmodifiable factors such as insurance type. Initially, we included insurance type in our multivariable regression model and engaged in extensive discussions regarding its role in healthcare. Recent literature suggests that public insurance is highly correlated with race, socioeconomic status, comorbidities, and chronic diseases. For this reason, we decided to remove insurance from the final model. Nevertheless, we agree that insurance is an important factor in its own role. We will include it in our multivariable regression model.
